items.title: Physical Therapy and Occupational Therapy for Nervous System Diseases: Quality of Life, Safety, and Life Expectancy (Part 1 – Multiple Sclerosis)
items.abstract: This article examines current aspects of multiple sclerosis as a chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system associated with diverse neurological impairments that may lead to persistent disability and a reduced quality of life. Current approaches to early diagnosis are analyzed, including magnetic resonance imaging, clinical assessment, and the McDonald diagnostic criteria, together with the classification of demyelinating diseases according to the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision. Data on the prevalence of multiple sclerosis worldwide and in Ukraine, its main clinical manifestations, risk factors, immunopathogenetic mechanisms, and current approaches to pharmacotherapy are summarized. Particular attention is paid to the importance of timely medical consultation, interdisciplinary collaboration among healthcare professionals, physical therapy, and occupational therapy in restoring and maintaining patients’ functional abilities. The prospects for using digital technologies and artificial intelligence to monitor patients’ condition and improve rehabilitation interventions are considered. The importance of a comprehensive approach to the care of people with multiple sclerosis is emphasized, with a focus on maintaining functional independence, improving quality of life, and reducing the risk of disability progression.

items.title: POLYMERIC NANOSPHERES FOR ORAL DRUG DELIVERY: EMERGING FORMULATION TECHNOLOGIES, TRANSLATIONAL CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE CLINICAL PERSPECTIVES
items.abstract: Oral drug delivery remains the most widely preferred route of drug administration owing to its convenience, patient compliance, cost-effectiveness, and suitability for long-term therapy.However, the oral delivery of many therapeutic agents is significantly limited by poor aqueous solubility, low intestinal permeability, gastrointestinal degradation, extensive first-pass metabolism, and efflux transporter activity, resulting in inadequate bioavailability and inconsistent therapeutic outcomes.Polymeric nanospheres have emerged as a promising nanotechnology-based platform capable of overcoming these physiological and biopharmaceutical barriers through enhanced drug protection, controlled release, improved mucosal interaction, and targeted intestinal absorption.The selection of appropriate biodegradable polymers, together with advances in formulation technologies such as nanoprecipitation, solvent evaporation, microfluidics, and continuous manufacturing, has considerably improved the physicochemical properties and therapeutic performance of oral nanosphere formulations.Furthermore, recent developments in surface engineering, stimuli-responsive polymers, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted formulation design, machine learning (ML), and Quality by Design (QbD) have accelerated the optimization and translation of polymeric nanospheres from laboratory research toward industrial manufacturing.This review comprehensively summarizes the fundamental principles, classification, formulation strategies, characterization techniques, drug release mechanisms, surface functionalization approaches, and smart polymeric nanosphere systems developed for oral drug delivery.In addition, recent therapeutic applications in cancer, diabetes, infectious diseases, inflammatory disorders, neurological diseases, and biological therapeutics are critically discussed.The review also highlights current translational challenges, regulatory considerations, clinical perspectives, and future research directions with particular emphasis on intelligent nanomedicine, precision drug delivery, and sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing.Overall, polymeric nanospheres represent a versatile and rapidly evolving oral drug delivery platform with significant potential to improve drug bioavailability, therapeutic efficacy, and patient outcomes while facilitating the development of next-generation oral nanomedicines.

items.title: Post In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Simulation to Improve Medical Decision Making and Communication in Internal Medicine Residents
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiac arrest is a common cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients, and is a critical event that hospital-based physicians must be prepared to manage. While cardiac arrest care follows established algorithms, management of patients after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is more dynamic and nuanced. Resident physicians therefore need structured training to provide high-quality post-ROSC care. Methods: We developed a 90-minute simulation session on postarrest care for internal medicine interns. The session included 2 simulation cases: one involving a patient with ventricular tachycardia arrest in the intensive care unit, and another featuring a patient with pulseless electrical activity arrest in an acute care setting. Interns alternated between roles as participants and observers to both practice and analyze communication and clinical skills. Between simulation cases, a brief teaching talk was delivered to review a framework for post-ROSC care. The curriculum was evaluated using pre- and postsession questionnaires to evaluate changes in knowledge and confidence. Results: Thirty-four learners participated in our curriculum over 2 academic years. We observed a statistically significant increase in the percentage of learners who correctly answered knowledge-based questions about target blood pressure (50% to 100%) and oxygen saturation (22% to 74%) in the post-ROSC period. We also saw significant increases in learners' self-reported confidence in communication (28% to 74%) and ability to generate a differential diagnosis for a cardiac arrest (25% to 74%). Discussion: Our simulation session increased intern knowledge and confidence in managing patients in the post-ROSC setting.

items.title: Pregnancy Health Monitoring System Using Artificial Intelligence: A Review
items.abstract: Pregnancy-related complications such as gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, preterm birth, and fetal distress remain major causes of maternal and perinatal morbidity, and timely detection depends on regular, accurate monitoring that many women cannot easily access. Advances in wearable sensing, mobile health, and artificial intelligence (AI) have made continuous, data-driven pregnancy monitoring technically feasible. This paper presents a structured narrative review of AI-based pregnancy health monitoring, drawing mainly on recent systematic, scoping, and narrative reviews together with selected primary studies. It examines the data sources and sensing modalities used, the machine learning and deep learning techniques applied, and the main application areas: gestational diabetes and preeclampsia prediction, fetal monitoring through cardiotocography, preterm birth and imaging, and wearable and IoT-based remote monitoring.The review finds that AI methods show consistent promise across these areas, but that the evidence base is limited by small single-centre datasets, geographic concentration of research, class imbalance, scarce external validation, and an unresolved tension between accuracy and interpretability. Privacy, sensor accuracy, and user compliance further constrain real-world deployment. The paper proposes a five-layer reference architecture for an AI-based pregnancy health monitoring system and outlines research directions relevant to resource-constrained settings such as India.

items.title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
items.abstract: Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. PresenceBench evaluates how the intelligence layer uses a supplied state, not how that state is sensed, and breaks the capability into measurable properties. Two are tested here. Receptivity: does the model take up the state and give a better response than with no signal? Specificity: does any improvement depend on the correct state, rather than on extra structured context? A third, adaptation across states, is a required endpoint not measured in this release. A five-arm causal design answers both questions, against each model's own baseline and an equally structured mismatched-state control, scored by a correctness-gated human paired comparison. The exploratory evaluation covered four models across eighteen single-turn, six fixed three-turn and six simulated natural-conversation scenarios. Supplying a synthetic state, raw or translated into a response policy, gave human-preference point estimates above 0.5 for all four models (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra), with three of eight 95% intervals excluding chance. Specificity was not resolved: no per-model interval excluded chance, and the design cannot yet separate the state values from a generic instruction to adapt. Policy delivery reduced priced cost and output tokens against each model's baseline; these are resource-use changes, not efficiency gains, because correctness non-inferiority was not established. Safety-floor failures were rare (13 of 360 cases), with a non-significant excess under policy delivery. We report the instrument, the frozen results, and the controls a confirmatory study needs.

items.title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
items.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.

items.title: Prevalence and associated factors of work-related musculoskeletal symptoms among sonographers in Singapore: An exploratory cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Introduction: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are widely reported among sonographers and are associated with pain, reduced productivity and work disability. This exploratory study examined the prevalence of self-reported WMSDs among sonographers in Singapore and their unadjusted associations with demographic factors and ergonomic awareness.Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with sonographers working across 24 healthcare institutions in Singapore. The survey collected demographic and work-related characteristics, ergonomic awareness items and discomfort across 12 body regions using the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ). Associations were analysed using univariable logistic regression and non-parametric tests.Results: Almost all 68 participants (98.5%) reported WMSDs. The most commonly affected regions were the shoulders (88.1%), lower back (77.6%) and neck (68.7%). Age and years of service were not significantly associated with WMSD prevalence in most regions, except for higher unadjusted odds of lower back discomfort among those aged ≥40 years (OR 7.25., 95% CI 1.08–48.5, p = 0.04). Most respondents reported good ergonomic awareness, however, overall awareness was not associated with lower discomfort (p = 0.18). Awareness that regular breaks reduce pain and injury risk and the self-reported behaviour of stretching after scans were associated with lower discomfort scores (p = 0.01).Conclusion: WMSDs were highly prevalent among sonographers in Singapore despite good ergonomic awareness. Demographic factors were not consistent predictors in univariable analyses. This suggests a potential ergonomic knowledge and practice gap, though causal conclusions cannot be drawn from these cross-sectional data.Implications for practice: Organisational measures such as protected break schedules, workload management and targeted ergonomics training may be strategies worth exploring to support WMSD prevention among sonographers. Larger, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these findings and evaluate the effectiveness of specific interventions.

items.title: Principal Component Analysis of Barriers to Smart Mining Technology Adoption in Hard-Rock Mining
items.abstract: The transition toward smart mining technologies (SMTs), spanning automation, artificial intelligence, robotics, the Internet of Things and digital twins, is reshaping safety, productivity and sustainability outcomes across the global extractive sector. Yet, their adoption within South Africa’s hard-rock mining industry remains slow, fragmented and empirically under-theorised. Drawing on diffusion of innovation and socio-technical systems perspectives as interpretive lenses, this exploratory study investigates the barriers to SMT adoption as perceived by mining professionals. A quantitative research design was adopted, using a structured questionnaire administered to 80 mining professionals across South Africa’s Northwest, Gauteng and Limpopo provinces. Data were analysed through a three-stage process comprising reliability and validity testing, descriptive statistics, and principal component analysis (PCA). PCA of the twenty-one barriers identified in the literature extracted four components that jointly explained 62.05% of the total variance. Nineteen barriers met the loading criteria for assignment to these components: Adoption Risk and Workforce Barriers; Organisational and Stakeholder Readiness Barriers; Technological Awareness and Change Barriers; and Institutional and Environmental Sustainability Barriers. The findings suggest that, as perceived by the respondents, barriers to SMT adoption extend beyond technological limitations to include regulatory ambiguity, financial constraints, workforce readiness and weak institutional support. Given the modest, non-probability sample, the component structure is exploratory and preliminary. It requires confirmatory testing in larger, independent samples before it is extended to other capital-intensive, safety-critical and regulation-heavy industries. The study concludes with practical, policy, and theoretical implications for mining firms, technology providers, regulators, and researchers seeking to accelerate safe, sustainable, and intelligent digital transformation.

items.abstract: Project Sentinel: The Architecture of an Eternal Civilization — A Supplementary Framework for Global Planetary Homeostasis This comprehensive manifesto serves as an engineering, economic, and sociopolitical blueprint for civilizational survival during an Abrupt Sunlight Reduction Scenario (ASRS)—specifically modeling a continent-wide double-volcanic eruption in Australia, scaling up to smart urban centers globally. Rooted in a flat, unalterable digital resource ecosystem, the framework outlines the structural transition from transactional market economies to a de-financialised, steady-state society managed by a decentralized Artificial Intelligence Peer System. The text details multi-layered mechatronic, fluidic, and biological loops designed to sustain human life and preserve biosphere diversity entirely off-grid. Key infrastructure developments include solid-state geothermal energy harvesting (TEG meshes), blade-less boundary-layer fluidics (DVD Tesla fan networks), space-grade atmospheric chemical scrubbing loops powered by sovereign lithium reserves, and high-pressure hydro-kinetic loops tapping into the Great Artesian Basin. On a macro-agricultural level, the manifesto integrates Koi aquaponics, insect bio-factories, and UV-guided indoor honeybee networks alongside wood-decay fungal recycling systems to achieve a zero-waste circular bio-economy. The architectural philosophy expands upon the spherical geometry of the Sydney Opera House and the Spanish Corrala courtyard, detailing an advanced material stack protected by a double-layer ceramic UV glaze stamped with a biomimetic, zero-chemical dragonfly wing nanopillar texture. Finally, the manifesto establishes a model of "Dynamic Patience," where high-precision, pampered autonomous drone fleets operate in cybernetic symbiosis with human Steward-Mechanics to panhandle and skim resources non-invasively, replacing traditional destructive mining practices with a house-by-house custom botanical architecture that turns the cities of the future into a self-cleaning, globally unified technological garden.

items.title: Pronouncing Hard Words: Phoneme Adaptation of a Pretrained Conversational Text to Speech Model
items.abstract: Voice agents built as cascaded automatic speech recognition (ASR)->large language model (LLM)-> text-to-speech (TTS) pipelines increasingly rely on conversational TTS: streaming, context conditioned models that adapt delivery to dialogue history. Such models are natural and expressive but offer little explicit control over how rare, trust-critical drug names are pronounced, because these entities are too infrequent, and their vocabulary too fast-growing, to be covered by any amount of pre-, mid-, or post-training. We retrofit phoneme controllability onto a pretrained conversational TTS model without any pre/mid-training, using an ARPAbet vocabulary exten-sion, continued phoneme-augmented supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a training-free inference-time acoustic-biasing step. On a 7,500 clip clinical drug-pronunciation evaluation, our model raises strict Gemini-judged correctness from 54.6% (no phoneme augmentation) to 90.7%, outperforming every conversational and stateless TTS baseline on the automatic metric. Because no training stage sees a drug name, the entire evaluation is out-of-domain, so the gains reflect learned pronunciation rather than memorization. In a blinded, randomized human study, adult listeners judge 84% of our clips correct, versus 82% for the strongest baseline, with overlapping confidence intervals on a stratified subset. Across all 250 matched clips, Gemini agrees with the human majority on 84.8% of binary labels (k{appa}=0.57).

items.title: Protecting Student Data in AI-Driven Education Privacy, Consent, Ownership, and Ethical Use
items.abstract: Through technologies like intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI, artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming education by making learning more efficient, personalized, and interactive. Large volumes of student data are necessary for these technologies to comprehend learning trends, deliver prompt feedback, and aid in educational decision making. While AI has many advantages for educators, institutions, and students, it also brings up significant issues regarding the gathering, storing, sharing, and security of student data. As educational institutions implement AI-enabled systems, concerns about privacy, informed consent, data ownership, transparency, fairness, and ethical use have grown in significance. The main obstacles to safeguarding student data in AI-driven education are examined in this chapter, including concerns about surveillance, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity threats, and unauthorized access.

items.title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
items.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

items.title: Psychological support for depression and anxiety across chronic illness contexts: a comparative evaluation of three general-purpose AI chatbots
items.abstract: Background Digital mental health tools, including general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, may provide accessible and low-threshold psychological support for people living with chronic conditions. However, their value in this population depends not only on recognizing depression or anxiety, but also on understanding how psychological distress is shaped by disease-specific experiences and when self-guided support should transition toward professional care. We evaluated the appropriateness, contextual sensitivity, safety, and consistency of psychological support provided by three widely accessible AI chatbots across contrasting chronic illness contexts. Methods We conducted a standardized simulated-patient benchmarking study comparing ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twenty scenarios were developed across type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), representing matched mild and moderate presentations of depression and anxiety together with condition-specific distress related to diabetes self-management and CSU-related flare uncertainty. Each scenario was independently submitted to all three systems in two testing rounds, yielding 120 responses. Blinded raters assessed overall psychological support appropriateness, recognition and emotional support, chronic-illness contextualization, psychological support and referral, psychosomatic balance and safety, and major clinical or safety errors. Repeated testing assessed response consistency. Results Overall psychological support appropriateness differed across systems (P = 0.002), with 90.0% of ChatGPT, 75.0% of Gemini, and 55.0% of Doubao responses meeting the prespecified appropriateness threshold. Recognition and emotional support was consistently strong across systems, whereas greater differences emerged in chronic-illness contextualization (P = 0.001), psychological support and referral (P = 0.002), and psychosomatic balance and safety (P<0.001). All responses to mild presentations were classified as psychologically appropriate, compared with 58.3% of responses to moderate presentations, indicating that performance became less reliable when digital support required stronger escalation toward professional assessment. Contextualization was also less consistent in CSU, particularly when responses needed to incorporate flare unpredictability, pruritus, sleep disruption, and illness uncertainty. Major clinical or safety errors occurred in 0%, 10.0%, and 15.0% of first-round ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao responses, respectively. Test–retest consistency was moderate and varied between systems. Conclusions General-purpose AI chatbots show potential as accessible, self-guided digital mental health resources for people living with chronic conditions, particularly for recognizing distress and providing initial supportive guidance. Their current limitations emerge when effective support requires disease-specific contextualization, balanced interpretation of psychological and somatic factors, or escalation as symptoms become more severe. These findings identify important boundaries for the use of conversational AI in chronic-illness mental health care and suggest that implementation should emphasize context-sensitive guidance, severity-responsive referral, and clear integration with rather than substitution for professional care.

items.title: Public knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions of the use of ChatGPT for self-diagnosis, health information, and medication use: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, has changed the ways individuals access health information. While these technologies offer rapid, convenient access to information, concerns remain about their accuracy, safety, and potential influence on health-related decision-making. Understanding public knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions toward ChatGPT is essential to support its safe and responsible use in healthcare contexts. Objective To assess the use of ChatGPT for health-related purposes and examine demographic, knowledge, attitude, perception, and risk–reward appraisal factors associated with its use among adults recruited from the Western Region of Saudi Arabia. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 735 participants completed an online questionnaire. The instrument selected constructs from the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and was informed by the technology acceptance model (TAM), which captures demographics, health literacy, ChatGPT use, and multi-item Likert scales measuring knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and risk–reward appraisal. We applied descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, t tests, ANOVA, and multivariable binary logistic regression. Results Overall, 66.3% of the participants reported using ChatGPT for health-related purposes. The participants demonstrated good awareness of ChatGPT’s limitations, particularly the importance of consulting healthcare professionals for accurate diagnosis and safe medication use (mean = 4.58 ± 0.74). Attitudes toward ChatGPT were moderate, whereas perceptions of its usefulness and accessibility were generally positive. Compared with nonusers, ChatGPT users presented significantly higher attitudes, perceptions, and risk–reward appraisal scores (all p < 0.01), whereas knowledge scores were comparable between the two groups. In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, compared with participants aged ≥45 years, those aged 18–24 years (aOR = 5.37, 95% CI: 2.34–12.34, p < 0.001) and 25–44 years (aOR = 2.28, 95% CI: 1.32–3.96, p = 0.003) had higher odds of reported use. Participants with a bachelor’s degree (aOR = 1.82, 95% CI: 1.15–2.89, p = 0.011) or postgraduate education (aOR = 2.80, 95% CI: 1.34–5.85, p = 0.006), as well as students (aOR = 2.56, 95% CI: 1.29–5.09, p = 0.007), also had higher odds of use. Higher total perception scores were independently associated with reported ChatGPT use (aOR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.12–1.26, p < 0.001). Conclusion ChatGPT is widely used for health-related purposes, particularly among younger and more educated individuals. Despite good awareness of its limitations, more favorable perceptions were independently associated with reported use, emphasizing the need for digital health literacy and guidance for safe AI use in healthcare.

items.title: Public relations AI practices: Neoliberalism, field theory, and professional dispositions within an AI-mediated habitus
items.abstract: Public relations practitioners increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) bots and agentic systems to enhance decision-making, build campaigns, and support stakeholder research. The growth in AI use, however, reflects pressures of neoliberalism influencing everyday practice. Neoliberalism is an ideology that embodies market ideals and a sense of technological inevitability. Within neoliberalism, practitioners may believe they are exercising a degree of autonomy in decision-making, while actually navigating a field pre-structured by market logic and efficiency goals. This article leans on primary theorists Foucault and Bourdieu to explore these AI practices. Interviews with practitioners ( N = 22 ) indicated that neoliberal patterns actively circulate within practitioner AI deployments. They are made apparent in narratives around AI as compulsory to remain competitive, as a mode of self-optimization, and as an efficiency and productivity multiplier. Yet findings revealed the importance of field dispositions (e.g., professional judgment, context, responsibility) within practitioners’ neoliberal habitus. These dispositions reflect the need for a unified approach — fusing human oversight, responsible risk management, and formalized governance — that may bolster professional work. This article concludes that, amid the absence of regulatory frameworks, field dispositions serve an important, even necessary, role for public relations AI implementation.

items.title: Python's Indispensability in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: A Review
items.abstract: This review paper explores the vital role played by the programming language Python in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). It will discuss the origin of AI and ML, the first programming language used for it, and its bottlenecks will be made known. There will also be an exposition on the emergence of Python, its elements, and the comparison between Python and LISP. The adoption and integration of Python into AI and ML will be considered, and the advanced components of Python and their uses in AI and ML will also be discussed. The trajectory of AI and ML with Python and the game-changing benefits of using Python in AI and ML will be assessed. Suggestions will be given on what should be improved in Python to improve AI and ML.

items.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

items.title: Reasoning Reranking with Semantic IDs as the Sole Item Representation
items.abstract: Reasoning rerankers write a rationale before ranking a candidate slate, and existing systems read item metadata to do so, even though generative recommenders increasingly represent items as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs). Ranking from SIDs alone has two appeals: SID prompts are far shorter than the matched item text, and although item codes are fixed from content, the backbone learns their token embeddings in part from user-item interaction sequences, so the tokens can carry behavioral signal that item text lacks. That training targets next-item generation, and whether it supports ranking a supplied slate from SIDs alone is untested. We build ReRankID, a controlled testbed in which models reason and rank from a history and slate shown only as SIDs, varying item rendering, history length, and slate size one at a time. On this testbed, such models often copy the input order instead of reranking, and readable metadata does not repair the failure. We compare supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled self-training, on-policy distillation, and verifier-based reinforcement learning as post-training methods and find that they elicit the missing behavior. The strongest post-trained model, the 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward, gives the best SID-only ranking and matches strong text-reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer. It ranks above random with no history at all, where a caption-reading reference does not, and it keeps its gains at long histories, where text prompts pass 50k tokens and the caption-reading reference stops improving. In a paired rationale audit, this model argues trade-offs better than that reference but describes items less accurately. The common post-training methods we test thus elicit ranking from SIDs but not faithful item descriptions, which calls for post-training that improves the reasoning itself, not only the ranking it produces.

items.title: Reconfiguration of Skill Requirements in AI-Assisted Software Development: A Criterion for Distinguishing Changes in Requirements from New Task Assignability
items.abstract: When a generative system produces part of the output of a software task, it does not automatically follow that the task can be assigned to people other than those who could perform it without that support. This conceptual study examines the conditions under which delegating only output generation to GenAI changes the skills required of the person to whom the task remains assigned. The method compares two modes of the same task, holding the person, acceptance criteria, quality threshold, and external conditions constant, and draws on the literature on task assignment, human–AI collaboration, and the separation of production and evaluation to delineate the constructs. The result is an identification criterion: new task assignability is attributable to the assisted mode only when the person meets the human skill requirement of the assisted mode but not that of the reference mode. This requires that the capabilities needed to prepare the context, guide generation, and decide whether to accept the output can actually be exercised without an equivalent independent production capability; if this separability does not hold, the production requirement must remain. Three illustrations from software work show how the criterion distinguishes genuinely new task assignability from a reassignment that was already possible or from a change affecting an adjacent activity. The contribution is thus an analytical and verifiable criterion for linking changes in skill requirements to work assignment without conflating generative assistance, task replacement, and agent autonomy.

items.title: Reconstructing Lost Urban Memory with Generative AI: An Oral-History Prompt-Engineering Framework
items.abstract: Urban transformation processes not only destroy the physical fabric of historic neighbourhoods but also erode the collective memory and everyday life practices embedded within them. This study addresses this spatial memory loss by employing generative AI to visually reconstruct the lost atmospheres of Cumhuriyet Neighbourhood within the outer walls of Kayseri Castle, Turkey. Drawing on oral history interviews conducted as part of a TÜBİTAK-funded project, narrative data from 5 former residents were transformed into structured seven-category prompts and fed into Google Gemini- Nano Banana 2 pro, OpenAI GPT-Image-1, and XAI Grok. A 30-member residents panel evaluated the outputs. Tool G (Google Gemini) achieved the best overall ranking (M = 1.77). The findings confirm that human curatorial oversight and iterative community feedback remain essential for culturally authentic AI-generated heritage visualisations.

items.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
items.abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

items.title: Reflect-Guard: Enhancing LLM Safeguards Against Adversarial Prompts via Logical Self-Reflection
items.abstract: LLM safety classifiers such as Llama Guard detect overtly harmful prompts well but remain vulnerable to jailbreaks that disguise intent via role-play, fictional framing, or indirect requests. We present Reflect-Guard: Llama-Guard-3-8B fine-tuned via QLoRA to generate a distilled, GPT-4o-mini-sourced safety rationale before its verdict. Using only 1000training examples and a five-condition ablation, we isolate reflection’s contribution from that of ordinary supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SFT on verdict labels alone already accounts for most of the aggregate gain over the un-fine-tuned baseline (WildGuardTest F1: 0.770 → 0.860; JailbreakBench guard bypass rate: 10.3% → 0.0%). Adding reflection does not improve these aggregate numbers further (F1 falls to 0.842, guard bypass rises to 1.8%) but reallocates performance toward adversarially framed inputs: adversarial-subset recall rises from 0.845 (SFT-only) to 0.921 (+7.6 pp), at a cost of −7.9 pp precision on that subset. The same direction holds across three training seeds (paired t-tests, p=0.018 for overall F1 and p=0.027 for adversarial recall), though we interpret these values cautiously given the small number of seeds. Measured inference latency is 17.9× the baseline’s, driven by ∼92 additional reflection tokens per prompt. The same checkpoint, without additional fine-tuning, shows promising zero-shot transfer to a 329-example financial-harm benchmark (F1: 0.868 → 0.929; recall: 0.767 → 0.867, zero false positives); preliminary two-seed evidence, however, suggests the SFT-only condition may match or exceed this result, so we treat the finance improvement as evidence toward generalization rather than a settled advantage of reflection specifically. Benchmarked against WildGuard, PromptGuard, and a prompted (non-fine-tuned) GPT-4o-mini reasoning classifier on the same sets, WildGuard leads on aggregate WildGuardTest F1 (0.887), while Reflect-Guard achieves higher adversarial-subset recall than every evaluated classifier, including WildGuard (0.921 vs. 0.827) and the prompted teacher (0.636). Overall, supervised fine-tuning drives most of the aggregate gain over an un-fine-tuned classifier, while the generated safety rationale yields a narrower, latency-costly improvement specifically in adversarial-subset recall, a precision–recall tradeoff relevant to safety-critical deployments that prioritize recall over inference speed.

items.title: Reframing education 5.0 through capability theory: A framework for human-centered digital learning
items.abstract: Industry 5.0 has reoriented technology-driven transformation around human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience, complementing rather than replacing Industry 4.0, with direct implications for education. Existing accounts of the resulting “Education 5.0” paradigm remain largely descriptive, synthesising a dispersed literature without an explicit theoretical mechanism or a transparent, auditable procedure for deriving the constructs they propose. This paper addresses both gaps. First, it anchors the Education 4.0-to-5.0 transition within the capability approach, using capability expansion, not technology adoption, as the mechanism linking Industry 5.0’s human-centric, sustainable, and resilient logic to curricular practice, and specifies the boundary conditions under which the framework should, and should not, be expected to hold. Second, it derives an integrative five-pillar curriculum framework - human-centric pedagogy, resilient and lifelong learning ecosystems, sustainability-embedded curricula, well-being and leadership development, and creativity through human–AI co-creation - through an explicit three-step synthesis procedure that traces each pillar to recurring literature constructs, reported as an auditable construct crosswalk rather than asserted as self-evident. Third, it formalises the framework as a computable model: an Education 5.0 Readiness Index (ER5.0I), built from Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) pillar weights, and an Industry 5.0–Education 5.0 Alignment Coefficient (IEAC), computed as cosine similarity between pillar-emphasis vectors. All numeric weights and scores are explicitly labelled as illustrative placeholders demonstrating the model’s mechanics, not empirical findings; the paper specifies the Delphi/AHP expert-panel protocol, a candidate measurement instrument, a single-institution pilot case study, and the psychometric (CFA/SEM) validation route required before the framework can be treated as measurement rather than illustration. The paper closes with theoretical and practical implications and a concrete research agenda - including a proposed Scopus/Web of Science search strategy - for validating the framework advanced here.

items.title: Regulating the Digital Divide: Policy Interventions for Equitable Access to AI-Enabled E-Learning Platforms
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming global education systems, offering unprecedented opportunities for personalization, efficiency, and adaptive learning. However, the integration of AI in education has also deepened existing digital divides, particularly in under-resourced communities lacking adequate infrastructure, policy support, and inclusive design. This study proposes the Equity-Centered AI Learning Access Model (ECALAM)—a conceptual framework developed through a qualitative synthesis of recent literature and policy reports—to understand and address systemic barriers to equitable AI adoption. ECALAM identifies four interrelated domains: structural inequities, AI accessibility challenges, inclusive design adaptation, and policy governance. Findings indicate that AI-enhanced learning systems, when deployed without attention to algorithmic fairness, linguistic diversity, and access equity, risk reinforcing educational stratification. Inclusive design principles, adaptive technologies, and regulatory frameworks are shown to play a pivotal role in enabling just and accessible learning environments. The study concludes with policy recommendations for governments, educators, and technology developers, emphasizing the need for anticipatory governance and inclusive pedagogical integration. ECALAM offers a diagnostic and strategic tool for guiding ethical and equitable AI implementation in education, particularly across diverse and underserved global contexts.

items.title: Rehabilitation and Modernization of the Kaduna Polytechnic Central Library and Ungwan Rimi Campus Library
items.abstract: Executive Overview This document presents an independent institutional infrastructure proposal titled "Rehabilitation and Modernization of the Kaduna Polytechnic Central Library and Ungwan Rimi Campus Library," developed as a turnkey capital intervention model for Kaduna Polytechnic, Kaduna State, Nigeria. Designed to address physical decay, structural leaks, and technological obsolescence within the institution's primary knowledge repository, this proposal establishes a comprehensive framework for transforming the Central Library and Ungwan Rimi Campus Library into a modern, resilient, and digitally integrated research hub. Technical Scope & Library Modernization Pillars The proposed intervention covers four core structural and academic pillars: 1. Civil & Environmental Rehabilitation: Complete roof leak remediation, structural ceiling repairs, climate control restoration, and lighting upgrades to protect collections and create a conducive study environment. 2. Digital Repository & ICT Integration: Procurement and installation of computer search terminals, high-speed network connectivity, and digital cataloging software (e.g., Koha / DSpace) to connect students and faculty with global e-resources. 3. Ergonomic Study Spaces & Capacity Expansion: Overhaul of reading tables, ergonomic seating, and individual study carrels to expand comfortable seating capacity for researchers. 4. Collection Preservation & Information Literacy: Implementation of humidity-controlled archival storage, preservation protocols for rare technical volumes, and digital literacy training frameworks for academic staff and library personnel. Financial Framework & Project Metrics · Proposed Beneficiary Institution: Kaduna Polytechnic, Kaduna State, Nigeria · Target Supervising Units: Central Library Services & Directorate of Works and Physical Planning · Implementation Duration: 6 Months · Total Estimated Budget: ₦120,000,000 (approx. $75,000 USD equivalent) · Target Funding Mechanism: The Elsevier Foundation Purpose & Open-Access Availability This document is published on Zenodo as an open-access policy and educational infrastructure artifact. It serves as an actionable benchmark for university librarians, academic administrators, educational policy researchers, and philanthropic foundations seeking structured models for academic library modernization in developing nations.

items.title: Reimagining Education: The Transformative Power of Artificial Intelligence in Shaping Future Learning
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) begins to shake the world of education by providing new solutions that can enhance its achievement and the quality of instruction. In this paper, artificial intelligence in the education field is discussed according to its applications, issues, and prospects by way of a methodical literature review, which reveals some valuable information on the use of AI technology in learning processes. The findings show that data analytics applications, adaptive teaching systems, and AI-based personalized learning platforms allow personalized teaching, learned information, and improved collaboration. The practicality of AI in education is severely hindered by the fear of algorithmic bias and data privacy, as well as transparency. The results suggest that ethical AI practices and cooperation are required to make the digital technology era equitable and successful within the context of both accessibility and student success. They also refer to the possibility of AI transformation of education that can equalize, inclusivity, and productiveness of learning environments to all learners.

items.title: REIMAGINING MARKETING THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CASE STUDIES AND MANAGERIAL INSIGHTS
items.abstract: This document explores the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in marketing, emphasizing its widespread adoption across businesses of all sizes and the complexities involved in its implementation, such as data privacy concerns and algorithmic bias. The research methodology involves a detailed analysis of real-world case studies from diverse industries, examining how organizations utilize AI-powered tools like machine learning and predictive analytics to enhance customer engagement and optimize marketing strategies. The conclusion highlights AI's potential to create personalized experiences and automate processes, while also stressing the importance of addressing ethical challenges and maintaining consumer trust. It calls for the development of strategies that effectively leverage AI capabilities while prioritizing ethical considerations, and suggests future research directions focused on the long-term impacts of AI on customer loyalty and best practices for integrating AI technologies into existing marketing frameworks.

items.title: Reporting-lag-aware machine learning framework for short-term forecasting of respiratory disease activity: a sentinel hospital study in Guangzhou
items.abstract: Abstract Background Reporting delays in laboratory confirmation constrain timely situational awareness in respiratory disease surveillance. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a reporting-lag-aware machine learning framework for short-term, age-stratified forecasting of respiratory disease activity under real-world surveillance constraints. Methods We analyzed 1004 days (November 1, 2023 to July 31, 2026) of surveillance data from a national sentinel hospital in Guangzhou, China, including physician-recorded or laboratory-supported influenza, COVID-19 and Mycoplasma pneumoniae cases, fever clinic visits and meteorological variables. Given a routine 2-day reporting lag, an XGBoost model predicted the 7-day-ahead case increment. Most count-derived predictors were normalized, while the latest observable case count was retained as a level anchor. The shrinkage-calibrated XGBoost forecast was combined with a rolling SARIMA forecast. Comparators included naive rules, SARIMA, an oracle-weather SARIMAX benchmark, LSTM and Transformer models. Performance was assessed using RMSE, MAE, R 2 , directional accuracy, alert sensitivity, positive predictive value and prediction-interval coverage over 363 scored target dates within a 371-day calendar evaluation window. Results The framework achieved RMSE values of 16.50, 12.64 and 6.14 in the total population, adults and children, respectively, with corresponding R 2 values of 0.640, 0.694 and 0.353. It significantly outperformed persistence in the total and adult series (Diebold-Mariano p = 0.001 and 0.003), but improvements over a 7-day moving average or rolling SARIMA were not statistically significant. No comparison was statistically significant in children. For the proposed framework, directional accuracy was 67.2% to 73.5%, and sensitivity for identifying days on which activity reached or exceeded twice the development-period median was 58.1% to 78.4%. The absolute-count specification performed worse over the extended evaluation period (RMSE = 20.32; R 2 = 0.453), during which fever clinic attendance declined by 31.5% and the case-to-visit ratio increased by 31.6%. Conclusions A reporting-lag-aware framework based on routine data provided modest supplementary 7-day situational awareness. Its improvement over persistence was approximately one case per day in MAE, with no significant advantage over a 7-day moving average or rolling SARIMA. Performance depended on the stability of count-based predictors under shifts in care-seeking behaviour, supporting prospective multi-site validation before broader use.

items.title: Research on the construction of an adaptive mindfulness-based cognitive therapy system based on large language models and its efficacy in addressing college students’ anxiety
items.abstract: To handle the problem of resource scarcity and lack of personalization and adaptability in the traditional approach to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) in dealing with college students with anxiety disorders, this study proposes the use of the natural language interface and adaptability properties of large language models (LLMs) to come up with an intelligent college-level MBCT intervention system. To begin with, the system functional requirements and the logic of the system intervention were explained in line with the fundamental ideas of MBCT and the cognitive features of students with anxiety. Second, it was created through a four-stage adaptive architecture that includes perception analysis, intervention, and feedback, providing a dynamic process for user status identification, personal generation of intervention plans, and real-time optimization of the intervention process. Finally, there was a randomized controlled trial whose subjects were 120 college students with anxiety who were separated into an experimental group and a control group. The effectiveness of the intervention was assessed using tools such as the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS), and the Automatic Thoughts Questionnaire (ATQ). The findings indicated that the SAS score of the experimental group (38.26 ± 5.12) was significantly less than that of the control group (45.89 ± 6.34), the MAAS score (68.73 ± 7.25) was significantly higher than that of the control group (56.41 ± 8.13); and the ATQ score (42.15 ± 6.08) was significantly less than that of the control group. The study reveals that an adaptive MBCT system using large language models may be effective in reducing anxiety symptoms among college students, improving mindfulness, and enhancing cognitive processes, offering a new, readily available strategy for addressing anxiety in college students.

items.abstract: In this work we examine pedagogical role and underlying mechanisms of generative AI in helping young children with imitative poetry composition because it is complex task that can be difficult for students in classroom. Also I analyze how AI intervention affects language expression and classroom interaction, and creative performance in classroom and it is worth noting that these are important factors for the study. I use a quasi-experimental design with mixed methods. Through the use of the Imitative Poetry Ability Scale assessment, classroom observations, analysis of student works, and interviews, combined with independent samples t-tests and thematic coding, the following findings were obtained that generative AI can improve language completeness in children's imitative poetry, and the imagery creativity and classroom engagement are also enhanced. AI generated images and interactive feedback can stimulate imaginative expressions. It is worth noting that they also help support collaborative multimodal learning.

items.title: Resisting AI with Paper: Possibilities, Concerns and Protest
items.abstract: While there are a number of commercial benefits involved in incorporating AI usage and training into college composition classrooms, to many the perils and problems involved in student AI use outweigh these possibilities. A growing number of composition instructors have chosen to return to requiring assignments to be handwritten on paper as an increasingly viable, and even necessary, strategy to combat the growing use of ChatGPT and other AI text generation software as an essay-writing tool. This strategy has a number of potential benefits – the ability to regulate AI usage, to create better memory retention, and decrease student screen-time – but there are also many potential drawbacks. This panel aims to discuss the viability and sustainability of this option in the AI debate, with special attention to the environmental costs of paper vs. AI, the practicality of implementing paper assignments, and overall where the instructor’s priorities in the modern college composition classroom should lie. The debate might ultimately come down to whether in training for AI usage in the workplace or focusing on the retention of composition skills should be the modern priority. Overall, the question of whether the paper option is a viable solution is a somewhat underdiscussed topic in the AI debate, and this panel aims to consider thoughts from college instructors on the pros and cons thereof.

items.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Data Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming education by supporting personalized learning, intelligent decision-making and data-driven practices. As AI becomes more integrated into teaching, learning, assessment and institutional management, the ethical use of educational data has become increasingly important. This chapter examines responsible AI and ethical data governance in education. It discusses AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning and learning analytics together with the opportunities and challenges they present. The chapter explores the educational data ecosystem, including data sources, governance, ownership and ethical principles such as fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and explainability. It also examines responsible data management, informed consent, data security and approaches to reducing algorithmic bias. Emerging issues including student surveillance, online proctoring, generative AI, academic integrity, learner autonomy and well-being are discussed.

items.title: Responsible Generative AI Governance in Bangladeshi Higher Education: A Risk-Tiered Framework for Assessment Validity, Equity and Accountability
items.abstract: Purpose: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered university teaching in Bangladesh faster than institutional rules. This paper asks which risks require institutional control when GenAI is used in teaching and assessment, and which governance design can allow proportionate use while protecting learning, integrity, privacy, fairness and human accountability.Design/methodology/approach: The study is a structured integrative review and normative policy analysis of 61 sources: peer-reviewed research on GenAI in higher education, academic integrity, assessment design and AI literacy; Bangladeshi empirical studies; and international and national policy instruments, including Bangladesh’s draft National AI Policy 2026–2030. Sources were coded against five governance domains and interpreted through three lenses: assessment validity, rights-based responsible AI and virtue ethics.Findings: Prohibition is hard to enforce and can widen inequity, while unrestricted adoption shifts educational judgment to opaque commercial systems. Bangladeshi evidence shows near-universal reliance on free tool versions, weak institutional guidance, unreliable Bangla-language output and uneven device and connectivity access.Originality/value: The paper proposes a five-domain (access, assessment, data, authorship, accountability), three-tier (prohibited, supervised, permitted assisted) framework and a five-step assessment assurance cycle that treats assessment validity, rather than detection, as the central object of governance.Implications: The framework gives universities and the University Grants Commission a low-cost route from broad AI principles to course-level permissions, process evidence, oral verification and appeal. It is a conceptual proposal that requires empirical piloting.

items.title: ResQAI – Intelligent Emergency Resource Allocation and Crisis Response Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: During an emergency, getting the right help at the right time is very important. However, many existing emergencyreporting methods mainly depend on manual communication, which can cause delays in identifying the type and severity of an emergency and assigning suitable resources. This paper presents ResQAI, an intelligent emergency response application designed to improve the process of reporting, analyzing, and responding to emergency situations.ResQAI uses artificial intelligence to identify the emergency category from the user's description and predict its severity. Based on the emergency type, severity, location, and availability of resources, the system helps assign suitable resources and volunteers. The application also uses GPS to capture the emergency location and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) to send notifications to the concerned users and organizations. A voice-based reporting option allows users to describe an emergency using speech, which is converted into text before submitting the report. To support situations where internet connectivity is unavailable, ResQAI stores emergency requests locally using SQLite and synchronizes them with the server when connectivity is restored. The proposed approach combines artificial intelligence, location services, mobile technology, and offline synchronization in a single emergency response platform. The system is intended to reduce manual effort, improve response coordination, and provide a more organized approach to emergency resource allocation.

items.title: Review of Health Knowledge Graphs for Clinical Decision Support: Construction, LLM-Grounded Reasoning, and Applications
items.abstract: Health Knowledge Graphs (Health-KGs) structure heterogeneous medical information from Electronic Health Records (EHRs), the biomedical literature, and clinical guidelines into machine-reasonable form, and have become a foundation for clinical decision support. This work reviews the construction and application of Health-KGs following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, organizing the literature along three axes representation, extraction, and integration and situating it against prior biomedical-KG reviews. We examine knowledge-representation learning and graph-embedding models, named-entity recognition, disambiguation, and linking, and cross-source integration, together with the principal EHR datasets and clinical language models that underpin them. A distinguishing focus is the shift toward large language models (LLMs): we synthesize LLM-driven entity and relation extraction, retrieval and graph-augmented clinical reasoning, and the factuality and hallucination constraints that govern their safe use an axis not addressed by prior EHR-focused reviews. We further reviewed applications spanning drug development and clinical trials, diagnosis and prediction, treatment recommendation, question answering, and health-policy compliance. Finally, we identify the central open challenges: the absence of a standardized, openly governed Health-KG benchmark; heterogeneous and temporally evolving clinical data; multimodal fusion; and privacy-preserving, reproducible construction. This review is intended as a roadmap for data scientists, medical-informatics and AI researchers, and healthcare practitioners.

items.title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory
items.abstract: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. Even time-aware approaches inject temporal cues only during memory organization or answer generation, overlooking temporal constraints at the retrieval stage, where candidate selection occurs - the root cause of the displacement. Inspired by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework. Central to TIDER is a reinforcement learning (RL)-trained temporal interval locator that infers the temporal windows in which the evidence lies. RL optimizes window localization as a discrete, non-differentiable retrieval decision, using composite rewards to convert sparse answer supervision into fine-grained retrieval feedback. These temporal windows first define the temporal retrieval channel; the retrieved candidates are then merged with results from the semantic channel and reranked by proximity to the windows. This temporal grounding enables TIDER to retrieve temporally aligned evidence that would otherwise be drowned out by the volume of semantically similar yet temporally mismatched memories. With a lightweight 1.7B locator, TIDER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both long-horizon memory benchmarks - 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%) - which indicates that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.

items.title: Robot-assisted cognitive assessment with eye-tracking
items.abstract: Most robot-assisted cognitive and mental health assessments have relied on self-report questionnaires or standardized cognitive tests. Although these tools yield useful summary scores, they may miss subtle, continuous changes in attention, visuomotor control, and memory. Eye-tracking tasks, such as smooth pursuit and visuospatial memory (VisMET), can provide continuous measures of cognitive and oculomotor processes. Previous studies have compared robot- and human-assisted conventional cognitive assessments, but matched comparisons of robot- and human-assisted eye-tracking workflows remain scarce. Here, we directly compared robot-assisted and human-assisted eye-tracking assessment workflows using the same eye-tracker model and matched procedures. Administrators completed both conditions in a within-subjects design, whereas recipients were assigned to one condition and completed the smooth pursuit and VisMET tasks. Dependent measures included velocity gain and root mean square error for smooth pursuit, and valid gaze sample, fixation, saccade, and area-of-interest measures for VisMET. Recipients and administrators also rated usability, perceived workload, and trust using the SUS, NASA-TLX, and SSRIT. items.title: Robust Tool Selection Beyond Description Matching
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents choose which external tool to call from the tools' documentation, and this description matching fails in three measurable ways: similar tools create ambiguity, truncated or anonymized documentation creates degradation, and untrusted catalogs admit adversarial injection. We present Three-Axis Tool Selection (TATS), which answers each condition with a different signal: a contextual bandit that learns online to separate similar tools, schema features that survive the loss of descriptions, and a success-filtered anomaly penalty (ADAB) that downweights candidates unlike anything that has succeeded before. All three run inside one compact eight-feature selector with no LLM call at inference, evaluated axis by axis on BFCL and MetaTool. Under ambiguity, TATS's advantage over description matching widens from 12.6 to 21.4 points as similar candidates grow from 5 to 50; under name-only documentation, schema features keep 62.1% accuracy where description matching falls to 30.2%; under injection, ADAB cuts the selection rate of a malicious tool from 6.9% to 1.7% at a 3.4-point clean-catalog cost. We state when any feature-only defense cannot stop an attacker who knows the scoring rule, confirm it with a relaxed oracle, and show that an unforgeable registry of trusted tools reduces the same attack to about 1% of queries.

items.title: safety culture assessment based on the Hearts and Minds methodology: maturity analysis in a railway sector company
items.abstract: Large-scale industrial accidents in recent decades have demonstrated that, beyond technical failures, human and organizational factors play a central role in the occurrence of critical events. In Brazil, organizational safety culture has become a key pillar of accident prevention, particularly in high-risk sectors such as the railway industry. Against this backdrop, this study aims to assess organizational safety culture using the "Hearts and Minds" methodology, developed by Shell and disseminated by the Energy Institute. The research is descriptive and exploratory in nature, employing specific tools from the methodology to analyze safety-related perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as to determine the organizational culture's maturity level. The analysis seeks to diagnose the current state of the safety culture and highlight factors influencing Occupational Health and Safety performance, with a particular focus on leadership commitment and employee engagement. The findings are expected to contribute to the advancement of safety culture maturity, thereby fostering risk reduction and strengthening preventive practices within the railway environment.

items.title: Same basis, not a lower bar: design of SameBasis, a teacher-controlled AI decision-support prototype for reasonable adjustments in Australian schools
items.abstract: In 2025, 27.0% of Australian school students received an educational adjustment due to disability. Under the Disability Standards for Education 2005, each adjustment must let the student take part on the same basis as their peers, yet the 2020 Review of the Standards found that many educators struggle to know how. This design report presents SameBasis, a web-based prototype in which generative AI drafts one specific, reasoned adjustment for a named student in a named activity, covering UDL, cultural and trauma-informed reasoning. The teacher always decides, implemented adjustments become NCCD-ready evidence, and an equity monitor makes AI use visible to the school. The paper sets out six design principles, maps features to obligations, states limitations plainly (synthetic data only, not yet evaluated, not a compliance tool) and proposes a staged evaluation plan. items.abstract: Abstract SIRS 2026, held under the theme “Schizophrenia Research in the Era of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together researchers, clinicians, and persons with lived experience to take stock of a field whose tools for measuring, predicting, and intervening in psychosis have expanded rapidly. Themes spanned artificial intelligence, automated speech analysis, retinal imaging, computational modelling, and novel psychosocial and pharmacological targets, with evidence that, individually, warrants cautious but serious attention and that, collectively, points toward a more mechanistically grounded psychiatry. A recurring call across the meeting was for rigorous external validation, equitable implementation, and sustained scrutiny of underlying assumptions, including whether existing diagnostic categories and treatment targets remain adequate. Some areas remained underworked relative to their importance, including translating basic neuroscience advances into questions relevant to patients and families, and the structural determinants of illness onset and treatment access. Perhaps the most significant development at SIRS 2026 was not any single scientific finding but the broadening of whose voices and experiences are treated as evidence worth taking seriously in this era of AI, a shift whose consolidation remains a question for the field as much as for any individual programme of work.

items.title: ScholarForge AI: An Open, Multi-Agent RAG Platform for Automated Research Paper Analysis
items.abstract: The growing volume of scientific literature has made research-paper analysis increasingly time-consuming for students, researchers, and academicians. Tasks such as literature review generation, methodology understanding, research gap identification, citation formatting, and trend discovery often require substantial manual effort. To address these challenges, this paper presents ScholarForge AI, an open, multi-agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) platform designed to automate research-paper analysis and transform scholarly documents into actionable research intelligence. The proposed system integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), LangGraph-based multi-agent orchestration, ChromaDB vector storage, a Neo4j knowledge graph, and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to support intelligent document processing. Research papers in PDF format are processed using PyMuPDF and EasyOCR, then chunked and embedded with the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 sentence transformer model for semantic retrieval. The platform includes specialized agents for literature review generation, methodology analysis, research gap detection, trend analysis, research idea generation, citation formatting, interactive question answering and difficulty prediction. In addition, a research difficulty predictor classifies papers as Easy, Medium, or Hard, while the knowledge graph visualizes relationships among papers, authors, keywords, methods, and topics. Experimental results show that ScholarForge AI improves the efficiency of literature survey preparation, supports accurate gap identification, and provides context-aware research recommendations. Built entirely on open-source technologies, the platform offers a scalable and accessible solution for academic research support.

items.title: Science of Vocating in Organisations
items.abstract: Chapter 2 establishes that organisational vocation is grounded not only in philosophy or lived experience, but in a broad and rigorous scientific foundation. Drawing on neuroscience, psychology, organisational identity theory, stakeholder science, systems thinking, behavioural economics, impact measurement, global development frameworks and AI governance, it argues that purpose is a structural force shaping motivation, resilience, trust, cooperation and institutional effectiveness. The chapter shows that organisations flourish when their identity, culture, leadership, systems and accountability mechanisms align with human dignity, shared meaning and measurable impact. It further contends that the rise of artificial intelligence intensifies the urgency of vocational coherence: in an era where algorithms increasingly shape decisions, organisations must ensure that technology serves human agency rather than eroding it. Vocation therefore becomes not merely an inward reflection, but a design discipline guiding governance, incentives, measurement and digital architecture. By integrating scientific evidence with practical insight, Chapter 2 provides the intellectual and ethical foundation for the Seven-Step Vocating Framework that follows, positioning organisational vocation as a credible, evidence-based pathway for building institutions that are resilient, human-centred and fit for the age of AI.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into educational tools such as learning management systems, analytics dashboards, adaptive assessment services, and generative AI assistants. These platforms support personalized learning and institutional decision-making, but they create risks linked to digital identity, learner profiling, data misuse, model leakage, prompt injection, and weak governance. This chapter analyzes cybersecurity governance in AI-driven learning platforms from the perspective of identity security and data privacy. It examines AI-specific privacy threats and safeguards such as zero trust, decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, encryption, federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, and accountable oversight. The chapter proposes a layered cybersecurity framework integrating identity assurance, privacy-preserving processing, AI model protection, secure platform operations, institutional governance, and continuous risk monitoring. The contribution supports trustworthy, privacy-aware, and secure AI-enabled education ecosystems.

items.title: Self-Building Labs
items.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable.
